## Proof

Since $m_j$ is unbounded and satisfies $m_j(x+y)=m_j(x)m_j(y)$, we first note $m_j(0)=m_j(0)^2$, so $m_j(0)\in\{0,1\}$. If $m_j(0)=0$, then $m_j(x)=m_j(x)m_j(0)=0$ for all $x$, contradicting unboundedness. Hence $m_j(0)=1$, and $m_j(x)m_j(-x)=m_j(0)=1$, so $m_j(x)\neq 0$ for all $x\in G$.

Define $f:G\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ by $f(x)=m_1(x)/m_2(x)$. Then
$$f(x+y)=\frac{m_1(x+y)}{m_2(x+y)}=\frac{m_1(x)m_1(y)}{m_2(x)m_2(y)}=f(x)f(y),$$
so $f$ is itself an exponential with $f(0)=1$. The boundedness hypothesis gives, for some constant $M$ and all $x\in G$,
$$|m_2(x)|\cdot|f(x)-1|=|m_1(x)-m_2(x)|\le M,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad |f(x)-1|\le \frac{M}{|m_2(x)|}.\tag{$\ast$}$$

**Step 1: There exists $x_0\in G$ with $f(x_0)=1$.**

Since $m_2$ is unbounded, pick $x_0\in G$ with $|m_2(x_0)|>1$. Applying ($\ast$) to $nx_0$ (where $nx_0=x_0+\cdots+x_0$, $n$ times) and using $m_2(nx_0)=m_2(x_0)^n$ and $f(nx_0)=f(x_0)^n$:
$$|f(x_0)^n-1|\le\frac{M}{|m_2(x_0)|^n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.$$
Thus $f(x_0)^n\to 1$. This forces $|f(x_0)|=1$ (otherwise $|f(x_0)^n|$ tends to $0$ or $\infty$). Writing $f(x_0)=e^{i\theta}$, the convergence $e^{in\theta}\to 1$ requires $\theta=0$, so $f(x_0)=1$.

**Step 2: $f\equiv 1$.**

For any $y\in G$ and any $n\ge 1$, using $f(y+nx_0)=f(y)f(x_0)^n=f(y)$ and $|m_2(y+nx_0)|=|m_2(y)|\,|m_2(x_0)|^n\to\infty$, apply ($\ast$) to $y+nx_0$:
$$|f(y)-1|=|f(y+nx_0)-1|\le\frac{M}{|m_2(y)|\,|m_2(x_0)|^n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.$$
Hence $f(y)=1$ for every $y\in G$.

Therefore $m_1(x)=m_2(x)$ for all $x\in G$; that is, $\boxed{m_1=m_2}$.
